strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple LLaMA models (7B, 13B, 30B) and diverse benchmarks, showing 0.2-0.5 PPL improvement and better zero-shot accuracy than strong baselines (SparseGPT, WANDA, BESA, LPAF)
Well-motivated problem identification with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches (manual thresholds, poor component coordination, lack of layer-wise redundancy adaptation)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, layer-wise analysis, and rank distribution visualization; detailed reproduction report with implementation details
Practical approach that automatically detects redundancy patterns across layers without manual per-layer hyperparameter tuning
Good reproducibility with code structure, hyperparameters, and thorough documentation of the implementation process
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: RPCA decomposition (Candès et al. 2009) and REINFORCE policy gradient (Williams 1992) are both well-established; the primary contribution is their combination, which is incremental for a top-tier venue

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem F.1 straightforwardly combines RPCA recovery bounds with PAC-Bayes without new insights; Lemma F.2 is trivial; theorem statement contains undefined O(·) terms without clear characterization

Experimental fairness concerns: (1) Main results claim 'no parameter updates' but Table 4 shows CAP only outperforms LoSparse with full fine-tuning (CAP4); (2) LoSparse comparison relegated to appendix using different model (DeBERTa vs. LLaMA); (3) Missing wall-clock time comparisons despite efficiency claims

Missing critical practical details: RPCA hyperparameter λ selection not specified ('default' undefined), RPCA decomposition time not reported, inference speedup not distinguished from parameter reduction, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters, and claim that dynamic hyperparameter updates 'yielded no benefits' lacks supporting data

Insufficient technical clarity on core claims: (1) How RPCA decomposition (Stage 1) constrains search space in Stage 2 not formally quantified; (2) Policy gradient uses 3 iterations and window size 5 without justification; (3) Claimed 'interaction management' between components appears underspecified; (4) Budget constraint enforcement during optimization not detailed
Limited architectural scope: Evaluation only on Transformer-based models; claims of model-agnostic applicability unsupported; no evaluation on CNNs, RNNs, or other architectures

Significant hardware acceleration dependency (Section G) insufficiently addressed: sparse matrix computation benefits depend on specialized hardware; practical acceleration not verified, limiting real-world applicability despite claims

Incomplete analysis and presentation: (1) Appendix A on knowledge neurons disconnected from main method with no concrete evidence CAP better preserves critical neurons; (2) Figure 3 shows unexpected last-layer performance boost with vague explanation; (3) Degradation at very high compression (80%+, appendix) substantial but minimally discussed; (4) Some redundancy in problem formulation across sections

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model scales and benchmarks with detailed results
Clear practical advantages of avoiding expensive iterative fine-tuning while requiring minimal calibration data
Well-motivated problem identification regarding limitations of existing low-rank plus sparse methods
Coherent two-stage framework that makes intuitive sense (decomposition to reduce search space, then adaptive selection)
Good supplementary material with comparisons against multiple baselines and analysis of learned structures
weaknesses: Limited novelty: simply combines well-established techniques (RPCA 2009, policy gradients 1992) without clear justification for why this specific combination is superior to prior work like LoSparse or LPAF
Marginal empirical improvements: gains are often <0.5 PPL without statistical significance testing, making it unclear if improvements are meaningful or within noise

Critical ablations missing: (1) no comparison between RPCA and standard SVD+magnitude thresholding, (2) no evidence that policy gradients beat simpler gradient descent on probabilities, (3) incomplete isolation of each component's contribution

Unfair experimental comparisons: different baselines receive different amounts of fine-tuning, with LoSparse comparisons relegated to appendix; CAP4 with fine-tuning clearly dominates but this conflates contributions
Weak theoretical contribution: Theorem F.1 is a straightforward combination of existing bounds (RPCA recovery + PAC-Bayes), not tight or insightful, and doesn't explain empirical performance

Underspecified method details: RPCA hyperparameter λ selection described as 'default settings', computational costs vague ('few minutes'), and insufficient justification for design choices (why Bernoulli distributions, why policy gradients)

Insufficient analysis of claimed 'interaction management' between low-rank and sparse components: the multiplicative independence in the final formulation appears weak compared to the claimed contribution
Limited practical scope: results degrade significantly at higher compression ratios (Appendix D), suggesting method has similar limitations to prior work without clear advantages

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in prior work (manual thresholds, poor component interaction, inadequate global rank allocation)
Practical two-stage approach combining RPCA and probabilistic policy-gradient optimization that avoids both heuristic thresholds and expensive backpropagation
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple LLaMA/BERT models with consistent improvements in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on diverse benchmarks
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of both components and sensitivity to RPCA iterations
Computational efficiency advantages: fast RPCA decomposition, policy gradient optimization on small calibration sets, comparable memory to WANDA while avoiding LoSparse overhead
Adaptive layer-wise rank allocation demonstrated in Figure 4, showing the method captures varying redundancy patterns across network depth
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines established techniques (RPCA from 2009, REINFORCE from 1992) without deep theoretical justification for why this pairing is optimal for Transformers
Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem F.1 provides only standard RPCA recovery bounds; Corollary F.3 is loose and uninformative; missing LLM-specific analysis
Incomplete experimental comparisons: LoSparse comparison limited to DeBERTaV3-base (Appendix B); LLaMA comparison dismissed as infeasible, creating significant gap with primary baseline
Results primarily demonstrated at 50% compression; diminishing gains at higher sparsity (Appendix D) limits practical applicability for aggressive compression scenarios
Sparse computation overhead not resolved: no wall-clock inference times or memory measurements provided; unstructured sparsity requires specialized hardware, limiting real-world deployment
Inadequate sensitivity analysis: RPCA hyperparameter λ uses 'default settings'; policy gradient uses only 3 iterations with unjustified hyperparameters (learning rate 0.05, window size 5)

Methodological concerns: RPCA iteration 1 achieves catastrophic 32497 perplexity (Table 2) with no explanation; Equation 17 scoring metric (probability × parameter count) is ad-hoc without justification
Limited mechanistic understanding: unclear why low-rank + sparse outperforms alternatives or which LLM properties are exploited; Equation 17 scoring lacks principled derivation
Scope limitations: focus on LLaMA/BERT; no comparison with recent methods (SLIM 2024); limited architectural diversity; comparison with BESA's blockwise allocation incomplete
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided; hyperparameter choices not fully justified; calibration set sensitivity (128 C4 sequences) not analyzed
